prediction:
THOUGHT: The patient is a 54-year-old woman with a painful, progressive, ulcerative leg lesion that began after an ant bite and has evolved over 1 month to a 4-cm ulcer with central necrosis and violaceous, irregular borders — classic clinical stigmata of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Key supportive features include: (1) pathergy phenomenon — lesion onset after minor trauma (ant bite); (2) comorbidities strongly associated with PG: Crohn’s disease (inflammatory bowel disease), prior corticosteroid-treated anterior uveitis (a form of systemic autoimmunity), and type 2 diabetes (which may contribute to impaired wound healing but does not explain the neutrophilic, non-infectious histopathology); (3) absence of systemic infection signs (normal WBC, no fever >38°C, normal platelets); (4) skin biopsy showing neutrophilic infiltration without evidence of infection or vasculitis — the hallmark histologic finding in PG (though nonspecific, it supports the diagnosis when correlated clinically); (5) presence of lower extremity venous insufficiency (dilated tortuous veins, pitting edema) — a common site for PG ulcers due to local trauma/stasis, though not causative. While other diagnoses must be considered — e.g., infectious ulcers (e.g., sporotrichosis, tularemia, or bacterial cellulitis/abscess), vasculitis (e.g., ANCA-associated), or malignancy (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma) — the biopsy rules out infection and malignancy; lack of systemic symptoms, normal labs, and absence of palpable purpura or other organ involvement make primary vasculitis less likely. Travel to Wisconsin raises concern for tick-borne illness (e.g., tularemia, Rocky Mountain spotted fever) or sporotrichosis, but those typically show different histopathology (e.g., granulomas, organisms, or vasculitis) and would not demonstrate sterile neutrophilic infiltrate. The combination of clinical presentation, pathergy, associated autoimmune/inflammatory conditions, and confirmatory biopsy makes pyoderma gangrenosum the most coherent and likely diagnosis.

DIAGNOSIS: Pyoderma gangrenosum
